SA NB 1. Agreement with SC Premier Properties, LLC
Recommendation:
Authorize the City Manager or his designee to enter into an agreement with SC Premier Properties, LLC for the return of parcels related to a 2006 Disposition and Development Agreement with the Lancaster Redevelopment Agency and execute all related documents.
The proposed agreement would allow for the return of this prime 27-acre commercial site to the Lancaster Successor Agency in exchange for the promissory note in the amount of $2,195,094 executed as part of the 2011 amendment to the DDA. The site offers substantial potential for future development, with the local real estate market continuing to heat up as the economy strengthens. This would not only provide the Lancaster Successor Agency with a valuable real estate asset at a time when values are on the rise, but also offer an ideal opportunity to leverage this site for future development, thus creating new jobs for local residents while increasing the tax base for the affected taxing entities.

Adopt Ordinance No. 1034, amending title 15 of the Lancaster Municipal Code by adding Chapter 15.46 (Electric Vehicle Charging Systems), establishing procedures for an expedited, streamlined permitting process for electric vehicle charging stations as required by Government Code Section 65850.7.
In accordance with Government Code Section 65850.7, the Ordinance provides that the building official shall implement an expedited, streamlined permitting process for electric vehicle charging stations, adopt the checklist described in the attachment, and ensure that the permitting process and checklist be published on the Cityâ€™s website. As set forth in Government Code Section 65850.7, the Ordinance also provides that electric vehicle charging stations approved by the City shall meet the requirements of the California Electrical Code, the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, and accredited testing laboratories, such as Underwriters Laboratories, and applicable rules of the Public Utilities Commission.

CC 9. Adopt Ordinance No. 1035, amending Title 10 of the Lancaster Municipal Code by adding Section 10.04.055 (Restriction of Oversized Vehicle Parking) to Chapter 10.04 (Traffic Code), to establish a general prohibition on the parking of oversized vehicles on all public streets, alleys, rights-of-way and publicly owned lots.
The Ordinance exempts certain oversized vehicles from the general prohibition, including commercial vehicles that are parked for the immediate pickup or delivery of goods, buses under certain circumstances, and vehicles used in other commercial activities. As introduced, it provides that an oversized vehicle may be parked in a residential zone while loading and unloading by an owner or occupant of a dwelling, for a period not to exceed twenty-four (24) hours. At the September 26, 2017 City Council meeting, the City Council approved the introduction of Ordinance No. 1035, changing the time period to seventy-two (72) hours.

PUBLIC HEARINGS
PH 1. Adoption of the City of Lancaster Master Plan of Complete Streets, Approval of General Plan Amendment No. 17-04, Amending the Plan for Physical Mobility and Other Associated Portions of the City of Lancaster General Plan, and Introduction of an Ordinance, Amending Portions of Title 16 of the City of Lancaster Municipal Code (Subdivision Ordinance) to be Consistent with the Adopted Master Plan of Complete Streets
Recommendation:
Adopt City Council Resolution No. 17-49, approving an amendment to the adopted General Plan, known as General Plan Amendment No. 17-04, adopting the City of Lancaster Master Plan of Complete Streets, and introducing Ordinance No. 1036, amending Title 16 of the Lancaster Municipal Code.
Over the last decade, the City has begun to consider other factors in the design and evaluation of streets. The understanding of the link between community health and active transportation options guided the City's adoption of both the Master Plan of Trails and Bikeways and the Safe Routes to School Master Plan; the development of both plans highlighted the need to re-evaluate street design to allow for safer environments for all users of the street, be they motorists, pedestrians, bicyclists, or transit users. The City's desire to revitalize the downtown area guided the redesign of Lancaster Boulevard, and it is clear that there have been substantial economic and social returns from the modification of the street design. Small incremental modifications to other City streets, such as Valley Central Way, have yielded significant benefits in the form of collision reductions even while traffic volume on the street itself has increased. These examples, combined with requirements by both the State of California and the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Commission to integrate complete, multi-modal streets design into local transportation planning, provide a practical, economic, and legal basis to revise the City's approach to street design.
